title: Can a fast wave pose as a slow one?
hook: Sample a fast wave too slowly. Which slower wave fits the same dots?

knows: digital audio is a list of numbers
doesNotKnow: that too slow a sample rate turns a fast wave into a slower fake

misconception: Sampling a sound often enough or not, the samples always trace the original wave.
objective: The learner can say that a wave faster than half the sample rate gives the same samples as a slower wave, so audio is sampled at more than twice the highest frequency.

claims.text: A 4 Hz wave sampled 5 times a second gives the same sample points as a 1 Hz wave; a 2 Hz wave does not.
claims.source: Node: cos(2 pi * 4 * n/5) equals cos(2 pi * 1 * n/5) for n = 0..5 (difference < 1e-9); the 2 Hz and 0.5 Hz waves differ at some n. Demo.tsx draws dots from the same cosine with f and FS = 5. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node: max |cos(2pi4n/5) - cos(2pi n/5)| over n=0..5 = 9e-16; 4 Hz vs 2 Hz differ by 1.12 and vs 0.5 Hz by 2 at some n. Matches stage dots (FS = 5).

claims.text: At or below 2.5 Hz (half the sample rate) no slower wave fits the dots; above it, a slower wave does (3 Hz looks like 2 Hz, 3.5 Hz like 1.5 Hz, 4 Hz like 1 Hz).
claims.source: Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem (Shannon 1949, 'Communication in the presence of noise'): frequencies above half the sampling rate alias to lower frequencies. Stage alias = |f - 5 round(f/5)|, node-checked for f = 3 (2 Hz) and 3.5 (1.5 Hz). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node over every slider value 0.5..4: alias(f) = f for f <= 2.5 and 2, 1.5, 1 Hz for f = 3, 3.5, 4, each passing through the same 6 dots (< 1e-9). Nyquist-Shannon: Shannon (1949), Proc. IRE 37(1): 10-21. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): node (fc12/check.mjs): for every slider value 0.5..2.5 no cosine below f (0.01 Hz grid) matches all 6 dots; 3, 3.5, 4 Hz match 2, 1.5, 1 Hz (< 1e-6). Phase-free argument: samples of A cos(wn+p) obey x[n+1]+x[n-1]=2cos(w)x[n], so w in [0, pi] is fixed by the dots; below half the sample rate no slower sinusoid of any phase fits. Stage message text matches. Shannon (1949), Proc. IRE 37(1): 10-21 (not opened; network blocked).

claims.text: That is why audio is sampled at more than twice its highest frequency.
claims.source: Shannon 1949 / any audio-engineering text (e.g. Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio): the sample rate must exceed twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Sampling theorem (Shannon 1949): sample rate must exceed twice the highest frequency; e.g. CD audio 44.1 kHz for a 20 kHz band.

claims.text: The stage samples 5 times a second (one dot per sample), names half the sample rate as 2.5 Hz, and shows waves from 0.5 to 4 Hz: an idealised cosine wave, not a real recording.
claims.source: Stage constants FS = 5 and the slider range 0.5 to 4 Hz in Demo.tsx. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Demo.tsx: FS = 5, Slider min 0.5 max 4 step 0.5, curves from Math.cos (idealised). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): Demo.tsx: FS = 5, dots n/5 for n = 0..5, NYQ = FS/2 shown as 2.5 Hz in the message and reveal, Slider 0.5..4 step 0.5, curves from Math.cos (idealised; no recording).

claims.text: Hz means full ups and downs of a wave per second.
claims.source: Definition of hertz (SI): one cycle per second. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): SI Brochure (9th ed., 2019), Table 4: hertz = s^-1, used for frequency of periodic phenomena (cycles per second). Stage predict text '4 full ups and downs a second' matches.

recall.question: A wave of 7 Hz is sampled 10 times a second. Which slower wave gives exactly the same sample points?
recall.why: 7 is above half of 10 (5), so it aliases to |7 - 10| = 3 Hz: the samples fit a 3 Hz wave exactly.
